utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next Prosecution witness is Mr. Caslav Golubovic, and his testimony is relevant to paragraphs 75(d) and (h) and 77 of the indictment. And he will be testifying as a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. The first person to ask you some questions will be on behalf of the Prosecution, that will be Ms. Kravetz, who is on your right. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Caslav Golubovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where and when were you born, Mr. Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1937 on the 15th of May in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now retired; otherwise, I had a degree in law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In 1999, Mr. Golubovic, were you the chief of the SUP or Secretariat of Internal Affairs in the town of Bor, Serbia?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Since when had you occupied this position?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: From 1982.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly where Bor is located.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Bor is in the eastern part of Serbia, close to the border with Romania and Bulgaria?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what is the area of responsibility of the Bor SUP?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the SUP of Bor covered the area of Bor, Negotin, Kladovo, and Majdanpek municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which police stations fell under this SUP, the Bor SUP?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Only the base in Bor, the Department of Internal Affairs in Negotin, the department in Majdanpek, and the department in Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that you're now retired. When did you retire from your position as chief of the Bor SUP?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of December, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And which rank did you hold at the time of your retirement from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I had the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning now to events that took place in April 1999, do you recall where you were on the evening of 6th April 1999 at around 6.30 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was in Bor, close to my house on the Bor Lake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall if you received a phone call around that time, on that date?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Around 1800 hours, Toma Miladinovic called me; he was chief of the criminal investigations in the SUP of Bor. And he told me that he had received some sort of dispatch from Kladovo that day and that something had happened in Tekija, in Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that Mr. Miladinovic called you and told you that he had received some sort of dispatch from Kladovo. Did he specify exactly what sort of information he had received?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that the dispatch said that at Tekija village, a refrigerator truck emerged from the Danube, filled with corpses, 20 to 30 corpses; that they had tried to recover the truck and perform an on-site investigation involving the municipal prosecutor and the investigating judge from Kladovo and a certain number of the police, of course; however, unsuccessfully. They did not manage to recover the truck completely, and it remained stranded on the bank. When he told me that of course, I told him to get ready. I found a driver, and we set out to go there and see what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did he tell you who in Kladovo had sent this dispatch, who had conveyed this information to him?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: He did not tell me the name of the person, but there is a standard procedure; whereby, the duty service from Kladovo sent the dispatch to the duty service, the desk, in Bor. And it was obviously something that belonged in the line of work of the criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: After receiving this information, did you and Mr. Miladinovic then head to Kladovo?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the driver arrived, I went from the lake to the town of Bor and set out to Kladovo together with Miladinovic, and that's about 110, 120 kilometres away from Bor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where exactly in Kladovo did you go to?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Even before we left Bor, I called up the chief of department in Kladovo and told him to wait for me at his office, that I was coming, and that he should have his men who had been working on the case that day with him when I get there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you called the chief of department in Kladovo. Who -- could you tell us the name of this person. Who exactly did you call?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Vukasin Sperlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you arrived to Kladovo, I understand you went to the police station in Kladovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who did you meet there at the police station when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: At that office there was a number of people from the station, or rather, the Department of Internal Affairs in Kladovo, that is chief Vukasin Sperlic. There was also Milan Stojanovic. It's really difficult for me to remember all the names now. There was the municipal prosecutor from Kladovo, the investigating judge, the president of the court who was in charge of investigations, as well as head of the centre from the State Security Service, together with another employee, plus another two men from the department of internal affairs in Kladovo; and I believe the commander of the border-crossing at Djerdap, and of course Toma and myself added to that number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Once you arrived at the police station, did you then have a meeting with these persons that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I had told them to wait for me there together with the head of department, of course I held a briefing in order to elicit information about the case and about what had been done until that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was discussed during this meeting, what information was conveyed to you about the developments in -- up to that time.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Sperlic briefed me that on the previous day, citizens reported that there was something floating in the Danube. On the evening of that day, it was reported to the Department of Internal Affairs in Kladovo. And one or two men from the department went on site to check out the reports. And if I remember correctly - it's been many years- they took a diver with them. And since that floating object was close to the bank, they just tied it in and roped it to a tree on the bank. Since they had a diver with them, they found out it was a refrigerator truck; and then dark fell and they stopped work for that day. On the next day, the 6th, an on-site investigation team took off from the secretariat, or rather, the department. They organised an attempt to recover the truck from the water with a crane, worked until noon or afternoon. They did not manage to haul the truck on to the bank, because the crane was not powerful enough. So the truck was hauled out only partially, and then the investigating judge came with the municipal prosecutor and proceeded with the first steps in an investigation. I was informed that when the door was opened, because the truck had its back to the bank, they saw bodies, 20 to 30 corpses, which they stated in the dispatch. They closed the door then. The investigating judge and the municipal prosecutor refused to perform the on-site investigation, because they believed it was within the jurisdiction of a higher-ranking court; and we were informed at their request. In the meantime, it got dark and work was ended for that day. And that's how we received that dispatch from Bor, stating the facts; namely, that a refrigerator truck had been partially recovered containing a certain number of bodies, and that they had informed the district prosecutor and the district investigating judge. And that was it until my arrival. After receiving this report given to me by Toma Miladinovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there, Mr. Golubovic, before you go further?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I think I have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is not an objection, but Mr. Golubovic said regarding the investigation that they always performed the investigation on the request, either of the investigating judge or the prosecutor, and that has not been entered into the transcript. And if you want, you can clarify it with the witness. And it should fall on page 46, line 2, after the word "request."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, can you confirm whether you said that you always performed your investigation on the request, either of the investigating judge or the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Under normal circumstances, that's what the regulations prescribe. The police come out to the scene, gather information, then the investigating judge conducts an investigation and directs the police what to do. In normal circumstances, when everything is normal - how shall I put it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Golubovic, you said that they informed you that they saw bodies, around 20 to 30 corpses. Were -- based on what the police staff at Kladovo was able to observe, were any assumptions made as to where these bodies came from?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? That was the first information that we received; and I think that on the first day, on the 5th, there was another dispatch. And in that dispatch the presumption was that there had been a traffic accident on that road along the Danube river, and that was the first assumption before the refrigerating truck or the object was dragged on to the bank. Our assumption was that up river a traffic accident had occurred and that that truck slid into the river. We had many -- on many previous occasions that the Danube on that spot would spout out bodies, vehicles, and years before this part of the bank was a channel for smuggling of contraband. So our initial assumptions were in that direction until the refrigerator truck had been partly recovered and until we hadn't opened the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And once you -- they had opened the door, what assumption did they make based on the observations of these bodies as to where the bodies came from?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: So that assumption that there had been a traffic accident was dismissed, and now the working theory that something else had happened. And this is why the dispatch was sent to the SUP of Bor. They asked for me, and they asked for further actions and steps because the municipal prosecutor and the municipal investigating judge did not want to proceed with the further investigations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you told anything about the truck itself, if anything was written on the truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: No. At that point, apart from the information about what had happened and what had been found, I simply wanted to take stock of the situation to see what is to be done next. First, I had received information what had they done that day; and, of course, I phoned my superior officer in the Ministry of the Interior, General Djordjevic, seeking further instructions on how to proceed in this situation, given that the court did not want to continue investigations. Although the district prosecutor had been contacted, none of them called back. So it was up to us to see what was to be done. I reached General Djordjevic on the phone. I briefed him about what I'd been briefed on. I relayed in a more succinct form what I had been told.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that you called General Djordjevic. Was he your immediate superior at the time?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: He was my superior. He was head of the public security sector in the ministry; and in wartime circumstances, during the state of war, of course you have to inform your immediate superior, whoever can be reached. He was available on the phone, and this is who I then briefed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you had contacted the district prosecutor and judge. From which jurisdiction were they that you thought would be competent over this incident?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that I contacted. I said that they were informed about the event, but they did not call back. Apart from the municipal prosecutor and the municipal investigating judge who attended that meeting, I had no contacts with anybody else from the judicial system. And the district prosecutor was reported as per regulations and as per reporting lines about this event.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this district prosecutor, which was the jurisdiction where he -- where he was operating?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: District prosecutor has the seat in Negotin, as well as the investigating judge. He covered the area of Kladovo, Majdanpek, and Negotin. The municipality of Bor was not part of that jurisdiction; it was under the district court in Zajecar, but he did cover Kladovo within his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that you called your superior, General Djordjevic. What was General Djordjevic's reaction when you conveyed this information to him?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I briefed him, and my impression of his first reaction was that he was also surprised, judging by the words that he uttered. And judging by his voice, I believe he was surprised by the news I imparted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall what he said to you during that conversation?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Since I sought instructions from him, he said that he'd be calling back, not for me to wait on an open line, but to stay on in my office until after he'd consulted the minister or somebody else; and then he said that he'd be calling me back with further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that he would call you back after he'd you consulted the minister. Which minister are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Minister of the Interior. Other ministers had nothing to do with this. Only the y of the Interior was in charge, and that was Djordjevic's ministry and mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who was the Minister of the Interior at the time?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the late Vlajko Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, did General Djordjevic call you back after you hung up from that first phone call?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: In some ten, 15 minutes he called back. He called and he told me to try to retrieve all the bodies, and at that initial moment that figure was known. He was taken to be known up to 30; and as per orders and arrangements that he made with the minister, that we were supposed to retrieve the bodies and bury them in Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did he give you any further instructions on how to proceed?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He just invoked the minister's authority and told us what to do. Given the circumstances, the state of war, and the fact that it was in the border area, we needed no further instructions. It was enough to be said to retrieve the bodies and to inter them, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did he say anything about what you were to do with the truck, the refrigerator truck that was in the river?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: No. At that moment we did not discuss that. Later on during the night, this became the topic of discussion; but initially in that first, rather, second telephone contact, this was not what we discussed. Because later on, the situation changed dramatically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you convey these instructions that General Djordjevic gave you to the other persons present at the Kladovo police station?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: They overheard my conversation because they were present around me. They listened to my briefing of the general and those people who were in the station, and I believe that judging by my reactions and my words they knew what the general had ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What steps did you and the Kladovo police staff take to implement these instructions?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we undertook measures to secure transportation vehicles, sheets, blankets. Because the people from Kladovo, as far as I was informed, since they thought that a smaller number of corpses were there, they had procured a smaller number of coffins; then we decided to depart from Kladovo to the place in Tekija and a criminal technician, criminal investigation technicians, and other operatives were supposed to provide the means for this action to be taken, for the bodies to be retrieved, transported. For that purpose, we took a truck from the municipal company to be able to perform the task. At a certain point in time, people tasked with this went to carry out their tasks, to provide vehicles. We took a service vehicle to the border police station at Tekija. That was maybe at 2100 hours, 2130, around that time; and then we departed from the Kladovo police department to Tekija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, other than the staff from the police station, who else was involved in performing these tasks of retrieving the bodies from the truck, if anyone else?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: A number of people from the municipal company, the funeral service municipal company in Kladovo, some five to six people. I never had interaction directly with them. I wasn't there. I'm not sure whether anybody outside the ranks of the police -- I believe that there was a number of employees of the municipal company taking part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that you departed from the Kladovo police station to Tekija. Where exactly in Tekija did you go to?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: We went to the key -- there is an office with a telephone line of the border police outpost, so that we may maintain communication and be close to the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you again report to General Djordjevic that night about the developments that were taking place?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was a report. I don't know how you interpret the word "informacija" or information. The first instruction, I wouldn't call it an order. An instruction was issued what to do when these bodies were being retrieved and transported to the truck that we had secured. It became apparent that the number of bodies were higher than the previously assessed number of 30. People from the scene reported back to me. I was in an office. I wasn't on the spot, and this of course changed the whole situation. I phoned General Djordjevic from that office again and told him and proposed, in essence, that we had no -- not sufficient resources to be able to carry out this task during that night, that the number of corpses was higher than previously presumed, that in the area we had no pathologists or people who would identify the bodies. So that -- that we could not perform this task. This was the gist of the conversation, and I proposed to the general and said, in essence, that it would be best for the bodies to be transported to a major urban centre, either Nis or Belgrade where there are top pathologists and where the proper examination investigation, under the rules and regulations, could be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately at what time you had this conversation with General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I presume, taking into account when we departed, et cetera, I believe that it was around 10.30, 11.00 p.m., around that time. The situation did not allow me to keep track of time or to keep a log of events. But taking into account the time of our departure and the steps taken, I believe that this was done approximately around 2230 or 2300 hours, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: By that time when you made this phone call, had you received any additional information as to -- from the persons that were at the scene as to from where these bodies could have come from, the bodies that were in the truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I had called general to tell him that I had received information from the scene, that the number of corpses was higher than -- than previously reported. The first presumption was 30. Now we figured out that there were maybe 50 or more, and that we had no resources to process this investigation and -- there at Tekija. And this is why I suggested that we should transport these bodies to a major urban centre, where there would be physicians and pathologists and other personnel who could conduct a proper investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Had you received any information as to the bodies themselves, whether there were bodies of male persons or whether there were also women and children in the truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Information that corpses were of both men and women was received by me during the briefing at Kladovo; and in Tekija in the office, there were people constantly coming in, coming out, coming from the scene, reporting on progress, on what had been done, and this is when I received such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did they tell you, these persons that were coming to you to report the progress, did they tell you anything about how these bodies were dressed, whether they were, for example, in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: They said that men wore civilian clothes of -- being of different age, that women were of different age as far as could be ascertained, and that they had the so-called billowing pants; although billowing pants are not worn exclusively by Albanians, but also Roma women and Serb women in Kosovo. But this was the gist of the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that some of the bodies had billowing pants which are not wore exclusively by Albanians. Are you -- by that time, had you made any assumptions as to whether these bodies had actually came from Kosovo or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was the assumption in the initial information that I received at Kladovo that the truck was, I believe, from Prizren. There were no number plates on it, but that it had markings from Prizren, Kosovo. This is the only thing that could be established at the time. A more detailed report on the truck or on the bodies had not been done. The assumption was that it came -- the truck came from Kosovo. There were markings of a company headquartered at Prizren, but this was not the most important thing to be done. At the time, there were more important considerations. So these are the assumptions that amounted to our impression that the truck came from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that you suggested to General Djordjevic that the bodies should -- given the number of bodies, they should be taken somewhere else, and I think you mentioned Belgrade or Nis. What was General Djordjevic's reaction to this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since the general initially reckoned with the initial number or the figure that I reckoned with as well, the discussion went about the point that it would be difficult to investigate this anywhere. But he eventually accepted my suggestion not to bury the corpses in the area of Kladovo, but to transport them by trucks to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did the workers finish unloading the bodies that evening from the truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: You know what? To cut a long story short, I must tell you that this was done under very difficult circumstances. The truck was some 30, 40 metres from the road. It was half drawn out on to the bank. It was very steep; and by midnight, we had managed to retrieve 30 bodies, only 30 bodies, that we placed on the single truck that we had available at the time. And this was it, as far as the job went that evening. So this was the number of corpses retrieved from the refrigerator truck on to the municipal truck. It was 30. Conditions were very difficult. We worked in the dark. There was no lighting. It was very difficult terrain, and it demanded quite a lot in terms of effort from the personnel who were performing the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Once these 30 bodies were loaded on to that single truck that you mentioned, where were they transported to?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I called General Djordjevic then. We had several telephone conversations on that night. Those bodies were transported in the direction of Belgrade. It was said they should be transported to Belgrade, and it would -- it was difficult for us to find the driver to drive the truck to Belgrade. I persuaded my driver to perform this task because there were no other drivers that could drive the truck, and we had received instructions to drive the truck to Belgrade. And during the night, maybe half past 2.00 or 3.00, it departed from Tekija through Milanovac towards Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you persuaded your driver to perform this task. Could you give us the name of your driver?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubinko Ursuljanovic was the name of the driver. He was my driver. He had a driver's permit for different categories of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did your driver tell you where, in Belgrade, he transported these bodies to?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement was when he departed - I spoke to either General Djordjevic or somebody else who answered the phone - for Ljubinko, the driver, to be met by somebody at the entry to Belgrade, since Belgrade had been bombed these days, and to lead Ljubinko through Belgrade streets to the final destination. I also sent a traffic police control consisting of two policemen to escort the truck to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did your driver tell you where in Belgrade -- what was the end destination of the truck in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: When he returned the next day, he told me that a vehicle, a Volkswagen Golf, had met him at the entrance of Belgrade at Bubanj Potok. It was early dawn. He was escorted by that vehicle through Belgrade; and on the way to Novi Sad, he then abandoned the truck. And the truck was taken over by other persons unknown to him, and then Ljubinko drove back to Kladovo. And this is how he related this whole story to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that he had to abandon the truck and it was then taken over by other persons. Did he at some later stage return to pick up the truck from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: The truck was taken back some six or seven days later. Ljubinko left the truck carrying the bodies there and returned, and the truck was then - let me make sure - around 15th of April. I remember that we had an accident at Kosovo and the commander of the Majdanpek police station had been killed in Kosovo, and we needed that truck. And this is why Ljubinko went back to retrieve that truck so it can be used here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know where he retrieved the truck from?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with his words, he retrieved it from the parking lot of the Ministry of the Interior. I don't know the specific location. But since the Ministry of the Interior had many different locations around Belgrade, I do not know the specific location. I never took an interest in that particular information. We were called and told that the truck was available. He went over to retrieve it and drove it back, because that truck was owned by the municipal company. I never asked him about the details, where exactly did he retrieve the truck from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, that evening after the -- that night after the truck was driven to Belgrade, did you leave Tekija, Tekija border police station?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: After that, after the truck was driven off, I believe I had another contact with General Djordjevic. And since we had no vehicles out on the ground, I asked him to secure a vehicle so that we can use it on the 7th of -- the following day, to use it to transport the rest of the bodies to Belgrade. We remained there at the border-crossing outpost and made arrangements and agreements on what was to be done on the 7th, to carry out the task. We had agreed to find a higher-capacity crane to pull the refrigerator truck from the Danube, to get the vehicle, to arrive on the 7th, to be filled with the rest of the bodies. Everybody from the Kladovo department got their tasks; and around 5.00, 6.00 in the morning - I really cannot recall the exact time - I set off with Toma Miladinovic back to Bor. I drove the vehicle, and I believe that I arrived to my office, to my work-place in the Bor SUP at around 8.00. And all the other tasks that were supposed to be performed were performed to -- by the Kladovo department employees. So on the 7th, early in the morning, I left Kladovo. I -- there was no need for me to be there, because I had issued tasks about what was to be done on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were the remaining bodies pulled out of the truck that day, on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I received information by telephone that on that day they used a higher-capacity crane, which was taken from the plant at Djerdap, to pull the truck out on to the road and that the truck had arrived from Belgrade. In the evening of the 7th, the remainder of the bodies were put into that other refrigerator truck, which then went towards Milanovci and Belgrade. That's the information I was given.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many bodies were pulled out of the truck the next day?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information, although the people directly involved would know better, I believe the figure was 81 or 82 corpses. The exact figure should be either in some statements or other evidence obtained from the people directly involved, but I believe the figure was 82 or 83 corpses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This figure that you give of 82 or -- 81 or 82 corpses, were those bodies that were pulled out on the 7th, or is this a total figure that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: It is the total number of corpses in the refrigerator truck that had been extracted on the 6th and the 7th. That is the total figure of corpses in the refrigerator truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the truck itself, to the refrigerator truck? What did they do with the truck once all the bodies had been pulled out?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, or rather, the next day, the refrigerator truck, as I was told by the chief of department, was taken to the public utility company at Negotin. It stayed there for a day or two. In my conversations with General Djordjevic, it was stated that the refrigerator truck was to be destroyed. I believe that was its subsequent fate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who informed you that it had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, whether Sperlic or Toma told me that first, I don't know, but one of the two; or maybe Sperlic had told Toma and then Toma told me, or Toma spoke directly to me. I don't know. In any case, I was informed by the people who had been told to inform me about it, and a lot of time has elapsed. I can't recall who exactly, but one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know how it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I was told that they attempted to set it on fire, that failed; and then it was destroyed by explosives. It was taken to Petrovo Selo and destroyed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, at the time that this discovery was made of the refrigerator truck and all the bodies inside, was any information given by you or by others at the Kladovo police station to the public, to the general public, as to what was happening?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one provided any information. Given the circumstances when all this took place, the arrangement was that that information will not be forwarded to the public, so as not to disturb the public. It wasn't deemed a secret. It couldn't have been, because half of the citizens of Tekija saw the refrigerator truck themselves. But it was something along the lines, Let us not disturb the citizens. And the agreement was that no information was to be given to the press. It was a time of war, and it would have caused disturbance with the citizens; and speculations were already being made and that would be disturbing to the public.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You referred to an arrangement or an agreement that no information would be given to the press. Who made this agreement, or among whom was this agreement reached?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: The agreement was first reached between me and General Djordjevic in the sense of not giving away information to the public, rather than it being a secret; and then I ordered the same thing to my subordinates, given the agreement I had reached with General Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall who exactly you conveyed this agreement to, who you spoke about the agreement that you and General Djordjevic had reached?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: It was conveyed to the same people who were present in the office during my first conversation with General Djordjevic. Do you want me to specify who was there or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. So if I understand correctly, your -- this agreement between you and General Djordjevic was reached during your first conversation you spoke about earlier, when you were at the Kladovo police station. Is that correct? You have to state your answer verbally.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke a bit earlier about speculations being made. You said that it would cause disturbance with the citizens and speculations were already being made and that would be disturbing to the public. What exactly were you speaking about when you referred to speculations being made?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: We were also speculating the first day that it was a traffic accident, that it was a smuggling channel, that we interrupted a human trafficking route, and the public began speculating as well. That's why I said it would be disturbing. Everyone would have his or her own view and comment to make, and all this can lead to a disturbance for the public. That is why we discussed the sealing off of any information channels, so as not to reach the press. It was a time of war. It was not peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about different persons being involved in retrieving these bodies from the truck. How were these persons paid or who paid these persons?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: The people who were from the Department of the Internal Affairs in Kladovo, six or seven of them, and the operatives of the state security in Kladovo; none of those were paid for it. As for the people from the municipal utility in Kladovo, there may have been five or six. We gave them a per diem for the job done; we paid them, the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who provided you with the funds to pay these workers?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I asked Minister Djordjevic in the ministry for the money, and it was received as such. Somebody brought it from Belgrade. He gave it to me, and it was around 10.000 dinars at the time. He told me to distribute that money to the workers of the public utility company against a receipt, and that was how it was done. It was nothing unusual, rather quite regular and in keeping with our regulations. That was the regular chain of communication between the ministry and the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said earlier that the local prosecutor and judge considered that this -- this matter fell within the competence of the district prosecutor and judge from Negotin. Did they come to the scene while all these events were unfolding?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: No, nobody came. And the local prosecutor and judge did not re-appear. They were there the first day, and they stated that the district prosecutor is competent. They were informed by both them and us, but no one arrived. There was no contact. Nobody tried to reach me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know why the public prosecutor or the judge from -- investigating judge from Negotin didn't come to the scene?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were any efforts made to try to contact them regarding -- to inform them what was going on?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: They were informed about the event by the municipal prosecutor and court in Kladovo and by the duty officer of the Department of Internal Affairs in Kladovo. That is the way of providing information on events. As for the rest of their contacts, I mean the municipal prosecutor and the district prosecutor, as well as the two judges respectively, I believe they had direct contact afterwards. It would strike me as something usual; however, nobody contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know if the -- if an investigation was ever opened by Negotin authorities into this matter, by judicial authorities in Negotin into this matter?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I was retired in 2001. I believe I learned from the press that an investigation was undertaken, that some work had been done by the district court in Negotin. I also know that the Department of the Special War Crimes Chamber in Belgrade is working on it right now, the war crimes court. As for Negotin, I believe I learned that from the press. But nobody called me about it and I don't know much more about it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did you at some point become aware of a story that was published on this incident in a publication called the Timocka Krimi Revija?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: After the event, whether it was in 2000 or so, in any case, I found out that there was an article published in that review about the event; and at that moment, apart from that piece of information, I had no other. After a while, articles re-appeared in the review and elsewhere, and an interview was published with a diver who participated in the extraction of the truck from the Danube. Later on, in 2001, one could find it in other media in Serbia as well. This is what I learned from the press.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with General Djordjevic after the publication of this first article on this incident?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I called him, and I told him that it had been published. It was a rather unpleasant thing for both me and him. I don't know whether he conveyed that further. In any case, I informed him. I told him it had been published in Zajecar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did he give you any instructions on how you were to proceed after this information had gone public?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't mention any instructions. It was a conversation. I told him it wasn't the best thing for it to have surfaced, and that's it. We spoke on the phone. He didn't tell me what to do about it, and I didn't discuss with him whether I intended to do anything. We didn't touch upon that topic at all. We simply discussed this event and the unfortunate circumstances under which it had been published.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with the other persons who had been present at the Kladovo police station on the 6th and 7th of April, for example, Mr. Miladinovic or Mr. Sperlic?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: It is possible that I had had contact with them, too. Miladinovic was there on a daily basis, and our offices were close by. It is possible that we talked about it. I didn't pay much heed to it, and I certainly didn't record it in any way as to the time or place. I may have discussed it with Miladinovic. I don't know about Sperlic because he was a bit further away, but Milutinovic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Miladinovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] was there close.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, in 2001, did you become aware of the creation of a Working Group in the MUP that was formed and tasked to investigate this incident of the refrigerator truck?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about it because they came to interview me. I knew that the new minister established the Working Group, tasked with investigating the incident. They came and talked to me. I don't know at exactly what time. It may have been May or June; in any case, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you recount the same events that you have described here today to this Working Group when they came to interview you?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: It was a rather informal interview, for the lack of a better word. It wasn't only about the incident, but about other things. As for the incident itself, we spoke about it in general, and they asked me who there was and so on and so forth. After that interview, they put together an official note containing the contents of that conversation. Perhaps it wasn't as precise and in as much detail as we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, since these events took place in April 1999, did you receive any additional information as to where the bodies that were transported to Belgrade, where they ended up. What was their final destination?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Since I retired in the meantime, I could only access information from the press; and from the press, I learned that the bodies were taken to Batajnica. I never had any conversations with anyone about that, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no additional questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic, and Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Golubovic. My name is Branko Lukic, and I appear on behalf of General Lukic before this Tribunal. I would kindly ask you to assist us in trying to clarify a few issues which may appear unnecessary to you, since it was a part of your job. However, we have to establish things in much more detail than can initially appear. Today at page 52, line 16, when answering one of Ms. Kravetz's questions, you said that you did not receive any orders from General Djordjevic, but rather instructions. Regarding that, I would like to ask you the following. Is it correct that the police does not function pursuant to orders, but rather pursuant to the law?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We abide by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you were asked whether you were familiar with this fact that a Working Group was established, tasked with investigating the issue of the corpses found in the refrigerator truck in the Danube. Do you agree that the directorate of crime police is the one which should take action following information such as this? Would that be the proper body to address it?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: In ordinary circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the regulation under establishment of the MUP states that this administration is duty-bound to carry out investigations and all pertained actions concerning such grave offences. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need to pause between question and answer, since we speak the same language. I wasn't waiting because I was unhappy with the answer. We heard that the Working Group interviewed you. The Working Group was headed by the police Captain Dragan Karleusa. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that at that time you knew that the police Captain Dragan Karleusa was deputy chief of the Directorate of Criminal Police at the MUP headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that himself when he came. Up until that moment, I wasn't familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to try and clear up a thing or two concerning police ranks, and it is connected to Captain Karleusa's rank and his functional position of the deputy head of crime police. Do you agree that this the MUP hierarchy before the introduction of rank, the function performed by an official held primacy before any ranks are introduced?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: The appointment by -- or within the formational structure took precedence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the hierarchy of the MUP, after the introduction of rank, the working post held primacy? That is, the type of work carried out by an official.

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, before and after ranks were introduced into the police hierarchy, the function or the post occupied by the given official held primacy over anything else. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know of any cases in the MUP headquarters and out in the field that someone of a lower rank was superior to someone who was senior in rank?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: It may have been, but I have no such experience. I had contacts with people, but no one who was my subordinate couldn't issue orders to me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Could issue orders to me. Could the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that Branko was the chief of SUP. I don't know any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will have to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be unnecessary, but if you think it's necessary please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember that Mr. Vlajko Stojiljkovic appointed Branko Djuric as the head of the SUP in Belgrade, and he held the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: I know that he was appointed and that he was the SUP Belgrade chief. As for any other personal data in terms of years of service, et cetera, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that moment, holding the rank of major, he was General Sreten Lukic's superior?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if he was head of the Belgrade secretariat and if General Lukic was part of the secretariat of Belgrade, then he was his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one thing to discuss with you. In your statement - and for easier reference that would be page 5, paragraph 3 of the English version; and page 5, paragraph 3 in the B/C/S version as well - you said that you heard and saw testimony of Bosko Radojkovic before this Tribunal. And you say that he was mistaken in his evidence to the Court, in that you ordered him not to take any photographs concerning the refrigerator truck. You said, "I didn't issue him that instruction or order to him nor anyone else. I had never spoken to Radojkovic on the scene." Is it true that you did not say to Radojkovic not to take any photographs?

utterances.speaker: CASLAV GOLUBOVIC
utterances.text: There are two sub-questions within your question. The first sub-question concerns the fact that Radojkovic, while testifying, that he had already taken photographs, and there would be no point in me to prohibiting him from taking photographs because I arrived on the 6th in the evening, and Radojkovic took those photographs on the 6th in the morning. That order may have any sense from that point onwards, when I instructed people not to make the events public to -- known to the public. I knew Radojkovic and I saw him after Sperlic had ordered him to come into the same office and told him to provide the sheets, blankets, et cetera for the transportation of the bodies. It is possible, since we were all at the Tekija office and people were coming and going, that Radojkovic may have entered on several occasions and reported on the progress made. That's quite possible, but I really cannot remember. I did not focus on Radojkovic and my transactions with him. But on that night in Kladovo, I saw him for five minutes when he entered the office, together with Chief Sperlic, and when Chief Sperlic issued instructions to him what to do. And it is possible that he may have entered the office at Tekija and briefed on the progress of the works, but I really do not recall him particularly because this atmosphere was specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that takes us neatly to our lunchtime break, Mr. Golubovic. We'll be breaking now for one hour. If you would please leave the courtroom with the usher, he will take you where you can wait meanwhile, and we will see you in one hour's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- we don't have more questions for this witness, so he can be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there may be -- is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's even better than that, Mr. Golubovic. We do not require you to come back. That completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to bring to your attention as early as possible my concern that, Your Honour, we are not going to have enough witnesses to fill up all the hours this week. I anticipate we'll probably finish with the upcoming witness this session. Tomorrow, we have no witnesses scheduled then. We do have Mr. Kryeziu, who was scheduled for Thursday. He's arriving I think late tonight and, there's a chance we could put him on tomorrow, but he's a 92 ter witness. His total time would probably be two hours, even if there's full cross-examination. Wednesday, we have two videolinks scheduled in Pristina. And Friday, depending on the Court's ruling, we may have Mr. Loncar for a videolink. The only other possibility I have, Your Honours, if somehow we manage to get Mr. Markovic here this week, but I don't know what the chances of that are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You also have -- did you also not have someone else proposed for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your motion to amend the 65 ter list indicated that your witness Sterenberg was to be scheduled for the last week of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know there was an objection about him and I don't recall, but we've now scheduled him for I think the 11th of December, because -- and I don't recall if he was availability or it was in connection with a Defence objection about his testimony. We found ourselves in the situation of having to reschedule him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The disappointment for us, Mr. Hannis, is that the one reason I think you've been able to advance for getting into this pickle is the extended evidence of one witness, which caused the postponement of the evidence of another I think, who was scheduled for two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. General DZ got pushed off, because Mr. Tanic and others took longer than expected. And he could not return until later in the month. The other thing, Your Honour, if you want to hear. Earlier in the month, there was some question about whether or not we were going to have extended days later in the month, and Mr. Ackerman filed a pleading which at the time you indicated was premature because there had not been any Scheduling Order. When the Scheduling Order came out on the 15th, we found ourselves in the position of not being able to advance anybody. Most of the people were not available between now and the holidays and had been pushed over into the new year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you really are going to have to start working overtime in getting people to attend to fill the remaining three weeks -- or is it two weeks? Two weeks I think apart from this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we're in good shape for those last two weeks before Christmas, Your Honour. We have very substantive witnesses for whom I'm sure there will be extensive cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One thing we could do, of course, is alter next week's schedule to give you more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a possibility, Your Honour. Next week we have General DZ, who I expect will go into a third day. We have another insider from the MUP. I know -- I think Mr. Ackerman made a request that we not have any witness who touched too directly on his client, because of Mr. Ackerman's obligations in connection with an appellate proceeding late next week. And the last week we've got Mr. Sterenberg, K79, Lord Ashdown, and General Naumann. Let's see how far we get today and we will then decide what we're doing for the rest of the week, and see if we can make that arrangement today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have one other matter I would like to raise. The Prosecution have applied for trial related protective measures for a witness K64. That witness is said to be scheduled for next week. Is there any possibility that Defence could make a very expedited response to this by, say, Wednesday, especially if you are twiddling your thumbs tomorrow. Very well, response for K64 by Wednesday. The next witness, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is Bosko Radojkovic, and his evidence relates to paragraphs 75(d) and (h) and 77 of the indictment. And he will be testifying as a live witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radojkovic. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, please. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Bosko Radojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where and when were you born, Mr. Radojkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 5th of February, 1956, in Rudnik, the municipality of Gornji Milanovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Currently, I am a retiree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And before going into requirement, how were you employed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I used to be a crime policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where were you working prior to retirement as a crime policeman?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked with the Department of the Internal Affairs in Kladovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In 1999, is this where you were employed, in the police station in Kladovo?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe what were your duties there as a crime policeman.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the Department of Crime Police, and I was involved with forensics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And which duties did you carry out as a crime policeman involved in forensics there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: All duties and tasks which fall under the framework of forensics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your duties in early 1999, in April 1999, were you called to the scene in the Danube river near the village of Tekija?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Why were you called to that location?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: To carry out an examination following a report of a fisherman on the Danube, whereby he stated that there was a large crate in the water which resembled the back of a truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall the date when you attended the scene there at the Danube river?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was the 4th of April, around 1.00 or 2.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall what you saw there when you arrived to the scene?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Some 30 metres away from the tank, I saw something sticking out, and it resembled the back of a truck. It was white in colour, and one could only see its rear upper part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who else was present there, apart from you, at that location on that day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from me, Zivojin Djordjevic, a.k.a. Zika, was there. He is a diver. He lives in Kladovo, and I asked him to come along together with his gear so we could check what it was all about. I believe his first name is Zivojin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Djordjevic investigate in any way what was in the river?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not; however, he went down; and upon return he said it was a truck, that there were no bodies in the passenger booth, that there is no driver or passenger, and that on the accelerator pedal a larger stone is placed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What did you proceed to do once that you were able to identify this object as being a truck in the water?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We called in a crane from the hydro-electric dam at Djerdap to try and pull it out and investigate. It was rather deep, and it was getting dark; plus the diver had no underwater light, so he couldn't clearly make out what type of truck it was. Therefore, it was left for the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So were you successful in pulling the truck out of the water with this crane?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Only partially on that first occasion, and then we had to employ a larger-capacity crane, which we also borrowed from the dam facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Before you left the scene that evening, did you do anything to secure the truck so it wouldn't float down or be taken away by the current of the river?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe we placed a bucket or a buoy. I think he tied it to the truck using a rope so that we could identify it the next day, and we may have borrowed a cable from a fisherman nearby to tie the truck to a tree on the bank. I'm not sure about the cable, whether that took place that night; but in any case, we marked the place where the truck was, so as to be able to find it should the water take it away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where did you go once you left this location where the truck had been found?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the police station. Zika went home, and we awaited daylight. The next day at the police station in Kladovo, preparations were underway to use a crane so that we could start pulling out the truck early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you went that evening to the police station, did you report to your superior on your discovery of that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, because we haven't discovered much. We found a truck in the water and that was it. Therefore, I wasn't sure whether that evening -- yes, yes. A dispatch was sent by a colleague that a citizen reported that case in Tekija, that a team was dispatched, but nothing has been established and that the work is still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that a dispatch was sent by a colleague. Where was this dispatch sent, or to whom was this dispatch sent?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: He sent it to the duty officer of the secretariat in Bor, to the duty office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The following day did you return to the scene where the truck had been found?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Early in the morning, we returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "we returned," was this you again and the diver, or were there other persons also present there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was there as well as the same diver. There were some people from the hydro-electric plant, the people who were manning the crane and some workers. All in all, some 15 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you able to lift the vehicle out of the water?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We were, around noon or 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon, but only partially. We managed to extract the freight box. We managed to bring it to the shore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you take any photographs while that was taking place, while the truck was being pulled out of the water?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many photographs you took on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Around ten or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P594. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, Mr. Radojkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is depicted on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: This photograph was taken while we were trying to extract the refrigerator truck. You can see the freight box; its rear turned towards the shore. What you can see on the side, the black line which comprises a triangle with the upper-most part of the freight box. This is actually the water marking. That's how the -- how deep the truck was, and this is the part seen by the fisherman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when you pulled the truck further out of the water, were you able to observe any type of inscription on the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the door, there was a company name. There was a company name on both doors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you explain what exactly was written on the doors of the truck.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can try and recollect correctly. It believe it said, Pik Progres Transportation and Slaughter-house Prizren, and there was a fax and telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P598.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recognise this photograph, Mr. Radojkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is when we managed to pull the truck out for the most part, and there you can see the inscription on the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to see whether the truck had any licence plates?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: There were no licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did you notice about the back door of the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The back door of the freight box in its right-hand, lower corner had been broken, or rather, the freight box seemed to have been broken in to, in the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You say that the freight box seemed to have been broken in to. Were you able to see what was inside the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything at that moment because the doors were locked, and the opening was of such size that I couldn't see through. I couldn't see what was inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was anything externally visible protruding from the opening that you spoke about in the back door of the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You could see two legs and one arm, as well as parts of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P596. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, you said that you could see two legs and one arm. This photograph is in black and white, but could you indicate if it's visible on this photograph what you could observe from where you were, your position, at the time you took this photograph.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: One can see that the photograph was not the best one that could have been taken; however, you could see a leg protruding. The rest is too dark because of the shade, and I don't think the photograph is of best quality. However, you could see another leg and one arm, but protruding less than the leg you can see?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, there is a pen on the side of your screen where the photograph is being projected. Could you mark where you can see the leg protruding from the side of the truck. If you could just draw a circle, just ...

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: These are the toes, the large toe, the foot, and then up the leg.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I don't know if this exhibit requires -- needs to be assigned an IC number. It's just -- could we assign an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit IC113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, were you eventually able to open the back doors of the truck that we see there on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The doors were opened later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what did you find was inside the truck once you opened the doors?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: What I found was a number of corpses piled up all over the freight box. Most of them were in the front part, because when we were extracting the truck it was slanted. It was at an angle. Therefore, most of the corpses were closer to the passenger booth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who was present with you there at the time when you opened the back doors of the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the workers of the power-plant who were working on the extraction of the truck, there was Momcilo Sujiranovic, who is a crime scene technician; then Milan Stevanovic, who was chief of the crime prevention squad in Kladovo; then the deputy municipal prosecutor; as well as an investigative judge of the district court in Kladovo; and someone from the medical centre in Kladovo, a coroner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were all these people able to observe what was in the truck when you opened it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Once I opened the truck, not all of them could see inside. But later, those who were supposed to see it did; however, some people refused to take a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you inform the local judge and prosecutor who were there about what was inside the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I informed the investigative judge, because he came to the scene; and from that moment on, he was in charge of the on-site investigation. I told him there were corpses inside, and I can quote his words. He asked, "How many?" And I said, "I don't know. Many. Do you want to take a look?" And he said, "No. It is not within my competences. You should notify the district court in Negotin." Therefore, he did not look inside, and I don't think the prosecutor did either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you remain at the scene after this event occurred, that you opened the back of the truck, or did you return to the Kladovo police station?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I returned to the police station. We all did, except for the policemen who were left behind to secure the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And once you arrived at the police station, did you inform your superior of the events that had taken place that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We wrote a report, or rather, a dispatch sent to the SUP in Bor, to the duty office. And it was drafted by me and Milan Stevanovic, who was the chief of service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who was at the time the head of the police station there in Kladovo?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: The chief in Kladovo was Vukasin Sperlic, and he was informed. He received regular information, and we told him what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What was the reaction of Mr. Sperlic and the other persons there when you told them about your discovery?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: By that time it was already afternoon or it was getting dark. The first reaction was surprise and then what to do. What I need to stress is that we did pull out the truck, however insufficiently for us to be able to carry out any work. That spot is close to the power-station, and the water level changes during the night. It can vary as much as one metre; and when it goes up, our truck was back in the water again. Therefore, we knew that the next day we would have to pull it out further again. Since we managed to see what was written on the door and what was inside, we tried to prevent any leaks of information, particularly since it was close to the Romanian border. There were ships about 1.000 metres away from the spot, since this all took place during the bombings and the aggression against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you tried to prevent any leaks of information. Exactly can you explain what steps you took to prevent any leaks of information.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: We met in the evening in the office and discussed what was to be done. An idea was that we could say that some Kurds were in the truck. By that time, the workers present and some others were able to see the legs protruding, and we wanted to present that as the bodies of some Kurds, who some 20 days ago had been caught trying to cross illegally from Romania. We simply wanted to say these people were Kurds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "we wanted to say," who are you referring to? Who was present at this meeting when this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: I was there, then Sperlic was, as well as Milan Stevanovic, maybe Sujiranovic, the local policemen. There weren't too many, though. As to who suggested what, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what exactly was decided that evening about what would be done with respect to the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was decided that the sign specifying the number -- the name of the company to be painted over with the same colour paint and to mount Bor licence plates on the truck. We were planning to put on registration plates from Bor and to cover the Pik Progres sign, indicating that it was a company from Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
